questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Random Variables that Follow a Geometric Distribution
questions.problem:
Which of the following random variables follow a geometric distribution?

- The number of candies selected with replacement from a bag before selecting a strawberry-flavored candy.
- The number of messages received by a person before receiving a message from their boss
- The number of strawberry flavored candies in a bag
questions.worked_solution:
A geometric distribution is used to model the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable I follows a geometric distribution. Selecting a candy and checking if it's a strawberry candy is a binomial experiment, and the number of candies selected before the first strawberry candy is selected can be interpreted as the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

- Random variable II follows a geometric distribution. Receiving a message and checking if it's from the boss is a binomial experiment, and the number of messages received before receiving the first message from the boss can be interpreted as the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

- Random variable III does *not* follow a geometric distribution. The number of candies (of some flavor) in a bag is not a binomial experiment.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable at a Point
questions.problem: At a water bottle factory, every batch of $50$ water bottles has $4$ water bottles (on average) on which the label is upside down. If an inspector comes to inspect the water bottles, what is the probability that they will find the first upside down label on the $5$th bottle they check? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of bottles checked until a defect is found. On average, the chance of finding an upside down label on any water bottle is 

$$
p=\frac{4}{50}=0.08.
$$

So, the number of bottles that the inspector checks before finding an upside down label can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success $p=0.08.$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.08).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.08)^{x-1}(0.08) \\  & =(0.92)^{x-1}(0.08)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding the first upside down label on the $5$th bottle is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =(0.92)^{5-1}(0.08) \\  & =(0.92)^{4}(0.08) \\  & ≈0.057\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$
p=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

So, the number of rolls until a $6$ came up can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success $p=\frac{1}{6}.$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{1}{6}).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={(1-\frac{1}{6})}^{x-1}(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & ={(\frac{5}{6})}^{x-1}(\frac{1}{6})\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =f(2) \\  & ={(\frac{5}{6})}^{2-1}(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{6})(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & ≈0.139,\end{aligned}

questions.problem: A smartphone receives a software update that has a $60%$ chance of installing successfully on any given attempt. The phone keeps trying until the update installs successfully. Rounded to $2$ decimal places, the probability that the update installs successfully within the first $2$ attempts is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of attempts until the update installs successfully. Since the chance that the update installs successfully on a single attempt is $60%,$ the number of attempts required to install the update can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=60%=\frac{60}{100}=0.6.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.6).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.6)^{x-1}(0.6) \\  & =(0.4)^{x-1}(0.6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the update installs successfully in one of the first $2$ attempts is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X\in {1,2}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(0.4)^{1-1}(0.6)+(0.4)^{2-1}(0.6) \\  & =[1+(0.4)](0.6) \\  & =0.84.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of cards picked until a red one is chosen. Since there are $26$ red cards in a $52$ cards deck, the chance of choosing a red card is $\frac{26}{52}.$ Thus, the number of chosen cards before getting a red card can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=\frac{26}{52}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.5).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.5)^{x-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)^{x-1}(0.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 5) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4,5}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & =(0.5)^{1-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{2-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{5-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)+(0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)^{2}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4}(0.5) \\  & =[1+0.5+(0.5)^{2}+(0.5)^{3}+(0.5)^{4}](0.5) \\  & ≈0.969\end{aligned}

questions.problem: A writer is editing the first draft of a book. On average, each sentence has a $5%$ chance of containing a typo. What is the probability of finding the first typo in the $4$th sentence or later? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of sentences checked until a new typo is found. Since the chance of finding a typo in any sentence is $5%,$ the number of sentences checked until the first typo can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=5%=\frac{5}{100}=0.05.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.05).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.05)^{x-1}(0.05) \\  & =(0.95)^{x-1}(0.05)\end{aligned}
$$

We require $P(X\ge 4).$ 

To compute $P(X\ge 4),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X\ge 4)=1-P(X<4)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in {1,2,3}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(0.95)^{1-1}(0.05)+(0.95)^{2-1}(0.05)+(0.95)^{3-1}(0.05) \\  & =(0.05)+(0.95)(0.05)+(0.95)^{2}(0.05) \\  & =[1+0.95+(0.95)^{2}](0.05) \\  & ≈0.143,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, there are no typos within the first three sentences is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 4) & =1-P(X<4) \\  & ≈1-0.143 \\  & ≈0.857\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{2}{5}).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={(1-\frac{2}{5})}^{x-1}(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & ={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x-1}(\frac{2}{5})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P(X>3),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X>3)=1-P(X\le 3)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {1,2,3}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & ={(\frac{3}{5})}^{1-1}(\frac{2}{5})+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2-1}(\frac{2}{5})+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{3-1}(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =(\frac{2}{5})+(\frac{3}{5})(\frac{2}{5})+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =[1+(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}](\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =[1+\frac{3}{5}+\frac{9}{25}](\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =0.784.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of getting a star card after the third draw is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3) & =1-P(X\le 3) \\  & =1-0.784 \\  & =0.216.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A coffee shop tracks how often customers order a latte. On average, $30%$ of customers order a latte. Each customer’s order is independent of the others. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability that the first customer who orders a latte is at least the $4$th customer is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of customers served until a latte is ordered. On average, the chance that any single customer orders a latte is 

$$
p=30%=\frac{30}{100}=0.3.
$$

So, the number of customers before the first latte order can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success $p=0.3.$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.3).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={(1-0.3)}^{x-1}(0.3) \\  & ={(0.7)}^{x-1}(0.3)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P(X\ge 4),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X\ge 4)=1-P(X\le 3)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {1,2,3}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(0.7)^{1-1}(0.3)+(0.7)^{2-1}(0.3)+(0.7)^{3-1}(0.3) \\  & =(0.3)+(0.7)(0.3)+(0.7)^{2}(0.3) \\  & =[1+0.7+(0.7)^{2}](0.3) \\  & =0.657.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the first customer who orders a latte is at least the $4$th customer is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 4) & =1-P(X\le 3) \\  & =1-0.657 \\  & =0.343.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: In a medical clinic, a certain rapid test detects a particular infection. On average, $9$ out of every $300$ patients who take the test receive a positive result. Each patient’s test result is independent of the others. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability that the nurse will test more than $6$ patients before seeing the first positive result is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of patients tested until the first positive result is obtained. Since the chance that any single patient tests positive is $3%,$ the number of patients tested until the first positive result can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=\frac{9}{300}=0.03.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.03).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.03)^{x-1}(0.03) \\  & =(0.97)^{x-1}(0.03)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P(X>6),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X>6)=1-P(X\le 6)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 6) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4,5,6}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5)+f(6) \\  & =(0.97)^{1-1}(0.03)+(0.97)^{2-1}(0.03)+(0.97)^{3-1}(0.03) \\  & \,+(0.97)^{4-1}(0.03)+(0.97)^{5-1}(0.03)+(0.97)^{6-1}(0.03) \\  & =[1+(0.97)+(0.97)^{2}+(0.97)^{3}+(0.97)^{4}+(0.97)^{5}](0.03) \\  & ≈0.167,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, the probability that the nurse will test more than $6$ patients before seeing the first positive result is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6) & =1-P(X\le 6) \\  & ≈1-0.167 \\  & ≈0.833,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Random Variables that Follow a Geometric Distribution
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following random variables follow a geometric distribution?

- The number of times a die is rolled until we get a $4$ for the first time

- The number of times a $2$ is rolled when a fair die is rolled $10$ times

- The number of times a coin is tossed until we get a head
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A geometric distribution is used to model the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable I follows a geometric distribution. Rolling a die is a binomial experiment, and the number of times the die is rolled before $4$ appears for the first time can be interpreted as the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

- Random variable II does *not* follow a geometric distribution. Rolling a die is a binomial experiment, but the number of times that $2$ appears cannot be interpreted as the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

- Random variable III follows a geometric distribution. Tossing a coin is a binomial experiment, and the number of times the coin is tossed before the first head appears can be interpreted as the number of binomial experiments needed before the first success.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: An archer is practicing archery. On average, the archer has a $7\%$ chance of missing every shot he makes. What is the probability that the archer will miss for the first time on the $8$th shot? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = (1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of shots until the archer misses. Since the chance of missing each shot is $7\%,$ the number of shots  until the archer misses can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p = 7\% = \dfrac{7}{100} = 0.07.
$$

So, $X\sim\textrm{Geom}(0.07).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.07)^{x-1}(0.07) \\  & =(0.93)^{x-1}(0.07)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the archer will miss for the first time on the $8$th shot is 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=8) & =f(8) \\  & =(0.93)^{8-1}(0.07) \\  & =(0.93)^{7}(0.07) \\  & ≈0.042\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable on a Bounded Interval
canonical_examples.problem: A high school soccer team is playing a local tournament. On average, the team has a $10\%$ chance of getting a tie in every game. What is the probability that the team gets the first tie within the first $3$ matches? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = (1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of matches until a tie is obtained. Since the chance of obtaining a tie in any match is $10\%,$ the number of matches until a tie is obtained can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p = 10\% = \dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1.
$$

So, $X\sim\textrm{Geom}(0.1).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.1)^{x-1}(0.1) \\  & =(0.9)^{x-1}(0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the team gets the first tie within the first $3$ matches is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {1,2,3}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(0.9)^{1-1}(0.1)+(0.9)^{2-1}(0.1)+(0.9)^{3-1}(0.1) \\  & =(0.1)+(0.9)(0.1)+(0.9)^{2}(0.1) \\  & =[1+0.9+(0.9)^{2}](0.1) \\  & ≈0.271\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable on an Unbounded Interval
canonical_examples.problem: A company is conducting interviews to fill a job. On average, $35\%$ of applicants meet all the requirements. What is the probability that an applicant who meets all the requirements will appear for the first time after the $3$rd interviewee? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = (1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of applicants interviewed until an applicant who meets all requirements appears. Since the chance of finding an applicant who meets all the requirements is $35\%,$ the number of applicants interviewed until an applicant who meets all requirements appears can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p = 35\% = \dfrac{35}{100} = 0.35.
$$

So, $X\sim\textrm{Geom}(0.35).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.35)^{x-1}(0.35) \\  & =(0.65)^{x-1}(0.35)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P(X \gt 3),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X \gt 3) = 1 - P(X \leq  3)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {1,2,3}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(0.65)^{1-1}(0.35)+(0.65)^{2-1}(0.35)+(0.65)^{3-1}(0.35) \\  & =(0.35)+(0.65)(0.35)+(0.65)^{2}(0.35) \\  & =[1+0.65+(0.65)^{2}](0.35) \\  & ≈0.725\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, the probability that an applicant who meets all the requirements will appear for the first time after the $3$rd interviewee is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3) & =1-P(X\le 3) \\  & ≈1-0.725 \\  & ≈0.275\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
